runs.question: How does the NIST Generative AI Profile describe data privacy risks?

answer.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile treats data privacy as a risk that GAI systems raise in several ways, mainly tied to training data and what models reveal or infer. It also flags that the risk shows up across the lifecycle and in how people misuse these systems.

- **Training data and privacy principles:** Training can draw on personal data, and that use puts transparency, consent, and purpose limits under strain (The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation.).
- **Opaque sources:** Because developers rarely disclose their sources, users often cannot tell whether personal information was used (most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.).
- **Memorization and leakage:** Models can expose training data under attack. The profile calls this data memorization, and it can create heightened privacy risk even for data that appears in only a few training samples (during adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data.).
- **Inference:** Models may piece together data from different sources to infer personal information that was never in the training data. Even inaccurate inferences can harm people, and wrong inferences about PII can feed into adverse decisions (GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources.).
- **Cross-cutting classification:** The profile lists Data Privacy under misuse by humans and under ecosystem or societal risks, as well as technical risks (1 ) Technical / Model risks (or risk from malfunction): Confabulation; Dangerous or Violent Recommendations; Data Privacy; Value Chain and Component Integration; Harmful Bias, and Homogenization; 2) Misuse by humans (or malicious use): CBRN Information or Capabilities; Data Privacy; Human-AI Conﬁguration; Obscene, Degrading, and/or Abusive Content; Information Integrity; Information Security; 3) Ecosystem / societal risks (or systemic risks): Data Privacy).

Note: the search tool was unavailable, so I read pages 5–7 and 10–12 of the profile directly. The privacy section is on page 11 and I did not check whether the profile's suggested actions for privacy appear elsewhere.

The NIST Generative AI Profile treats data privacy as a risk that GAI systems raise in several ways, mainly tied to training data and what models reveal or infer. It also flags that the risk shows up across the lifecycle and in how people misuse these systems.

- **Training data and privacy principles:** Training can draw on personal data, and that use puts transparency, consent, and purpose limits under strain (The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation.).
- **Opaque sources:** Because developers rarely disclose their sources, users often cannot tell whether personal information was used (most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.).
- **Memorization and leakage:** Models can expose training data under attack. The profile calls this data memorization, and it can create heightened privacy risk even for data that appears in only a few training samples (during adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data.).
- **Inference:** Models may piece together data from different sources to infer personal information that was never in the training data. Even inaccurate inferences can harm people, and wrong inferences about PII can feed into adverse decisions (GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources.).
- **Cross-cutting classification:** The profile lists Data Privacy under misuse by humans and under ecosystem or societal risks, as well as technical risks (1 ) Technical / Model risks (or risk from malfunction): Confabulation; Dangerous or Violent Recommendations; Data Privacy; Value Chain and Component Integration; Harmful Bias, and Homogenization; 2) Misuse by humans (or malicious use): CBRN Information or Capabilities; Data Privacy; Human-AI Conﬁguration; Obscene, Degrading, and/or Abusive Content; Information Integrity; Information Security; 3) Ecosystem / societal risks (or systemic risks): Data Privacy).
